en: Composed by the Śramaṇa Zhànrán of Pílíng during the Táng Dynasty.

Regarding the second [section], the clarification of the union and separation of objects and wisdom: first, in the explanation of the Truths (*satya*), there is first the general and then the specific.
First, regarding the general introduction to the various sūtras: the various sūtras and śāstras differ in their treatment of the union and separation of the Truths; now, by means of...
This does not generally apply across the four teachings; rather,
it specifically applies to the Tripitaka as the lowest level, corresponding to each of the four teachings individually.
Regarding this, the initial section clarifies the combination and separation of two and three.
First, it clarifies that there are only two and no third;
next, from "The Bodhisattva... onwards...
The judgment regarding the person is based on the truths.
The initial passage refers to the conventional; from the section following "the subsequent mind" onwards, it refers to the ultimate.
This is precisely the truth.
Therefore, from beginning to end, there are only two truths.
As for the statement that "it causes the fat of afflictions to melt away," etc.:
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Although this bodhisattva possesses the five exquisite sensual desires, he does not give rise to greedy attachment,
because he maintains contemplations such as impermanence."
It is like a king who has a minister concealing his own crime;
the king wishes to punish him for that offense.
The King said,
"If you can obtain a fat sheep free of fat, I shall pardon your crime.
The wise minister tied up a sheep and raised it on water and grass.
Every day, at the three times of the day, he frightened them with wolves.
Although the sheep were thus nourished and grew fat, they had no fat.
The king asked:
How is this so? The answer is as stated above;
the Bodhisattva is likewise.
Seeing impermanence as a wolf causes the fat of the fetters to melt away while the body of merit grows stout.
Furthermore, when this bodhisattva has not yet severed the fetters:
Just as one would not kill a thief until he has been captured,
but instead keeps him securely confined in one place while attending to one's own affairs,
so too does the Bodhisattva cultivate the contemplation of impermanence.
It is also like confining a thief;
although still subject to outflows (*sāsrava*), one performs one's own tasks.
Furthermore, it is free from five matters.
First, one is freed from the evil realms;
second, one is freed from poverty;
third, one is freed from the female body.
Fourth, freedom from physical deformity;
fifth, freedom from forgetfulness.
One attains these five merits.
First, one will be born into a noble family;
second, one will be reborn among humans or devas;
third, one will obtain a male body.
Fourth, the perfection of the faculties;
fifth, the recollection of past lives.
These are the qualities of one who has practiced the six perfections for three asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
*Asaṃkhyeya*, here translated as "innumerable," refers to *kalpas*, which are units of time,
as previously explained.
The *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"Among the eighty [intermediate kalpas], there are great kalpas; a great kalpa consists of three incalculables (*asaṃkhyeya*).
This refers to the fifty-second number among the sixty numbers."
It is called an *asaṃkhyeya*.
This is because these great eons (*mahākalpa*), when accumulated, constitute an incalculable number.
Thus, there are three *asaṃkhyeyas*.
Regarding the practitioner of the six perfections:
when a bodhisattva cultivates these six perfections, each has its own time of fulfillment.
First, as for what is called the fulfillment of *dāna* (generosity):
In the past, when Śākyamuni Bodhisattva was a king named Viśvabhū,
he attained the *Namo-rakṣa-dhāraṇī* and regarded all sentient beings as a mother loves her child.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of Devas, knowing his life was about to end,
sought out the Buddha to inquire about his doubts; having searched everywhere without success,
he returned to his celestial palace, filled with sorrow, anxiety, and distress.
At that time, a celestial master craftsman named Viśvakarman asked the Lord of Devas,
"Why are you so distressed?"
He replied,
"I sought an omniscient person but was unable to find one. Viśva said:
There are great bodhisattvas who, having fulfilled the six perfections, will attain buddhahood before long.
The Lord of Devas answered in verse:
"The bodhisattvas who have resolved upon the Great Mind are like fish eggs and mango blossoms."
"Of these three matters, the causes are many,
while the results are very few.
Viśvakarman replied:
"Uposatha will soon attain Buddhahood once his fulfillment of the six perfections is complete.
Śakra said, "I shall go and test whether he is truly a bodhisattva or not."
"You became a pigeon and I became a hawk.
You then feigned fear and hid beneath the armpit of the king of men.
Viśvāmitra said:
"This is a great bodhisattva;
why would you trouble him with such matters?
Śāriputra replied, "I too have no evil mind, just as true gold must be tested."
Just as it had been described, he transformed and entered the king's armpit;
his entire body trembled with fear, and as he moved, he made a sound.
All the people said:
This king is greatly compassionate and worthy of protecting all;
thus, this small pigeon bird has sought refuge with him as if entering its own home.
Such are the marks of a Bodhisattva; it will not be long before he becomes a Buddha.
At that time, a hawk was perched on a nearby tree and said to the king,
"Give me back my dove."
The King said, "I previously accepted this pigeon; it was not you who previously accepted it.
I first made a vow to deliver all sentient beings."
The hawk said, "I wish to deliver all sentient beings; am I not also a sentient being?
Why then do you snatch away my food?"
The king said,
"What food do you require?
I have previously made a vow."
"If there are sentient beings who have not yet taken refuge in me,
I shall certainly rescue and protect them.
The hawk said:
"I require fresh meat and warm blood.
The king said,
"There is no way to obtain these without killing."
What is meant by "killing one and giving one"?
With a mind concentrated through contemplation, he spoke this verse:
"This is my physical body."
Constantly subject to old age, sickness,
and death, they will soon become putrid and rot;
I shall provide what they require.
He took a knife and cut flesh from his own thigh to give to him.
The hawk said,
"You must follow the proper principle so that the weight is equal."
"Do not deceive me.
The king said,
"Bring the scale and weigh the pigeon."
As he spoke and weighed them,
the pigeon’s body grew heavier while the king’s flesh grew lighter,
until finally his entire body was exhausted.
The ministers and relatives turned away the onlookers, saying, "The King is now like this; there is nothing left to behold.
The King said:
"Behold! If you would attain the path of Buddhahood, you must endure this great matter.
The king smeared his hands with blood and grasped the scale, intending to ascend it entirely in exchange for the pigeon.
The hawk said,
"Why do you use such means to return this pigeon to me?
The king said:
Having lost my body countless times, now is the time to seek the Buddha-way with ease.
With my flesh exhausted and my tendons severed, I wish to ascend but fall;
thereupon, I reproached myself, saying:
"You must remain firm and not fall into confusion.
Sentient beings have fallen into the ocean of sorrow and you ought to rescue and protect them; why be indolent?"
"It does not even equal one-sixteenth part of the suffering of hell. If I,
who am specifically diligent, still suffer from this pain,
how much more so for those in hell who lack wisdom?"
At that time, the devas praised him, saying,
"For a small bird to be able to do this!
Then the earth and heavens shook in six ways, and the waters of the ocean surged with waves.
Flowers bloomed upon withered trees and the heavens rained down fragrant water.
The Buddhas came to offer praise, declaring that he would certainly attain Buddhahood.
A hawk spoke to a dove.
"He is a true Bodhisattva," Viśvakarman said.
"O Lord of Devas."
"You possess supernatural powers; you can restore him to health.
Śakra replied, "There is no need for me."
The King made a vow that moved all beings.
Śakra addressed the King, saying,
"Is your mind not distressed?"
The King said, "My heart is joyful; it is neither troubled nor submerged.
Śāriputra explained:
"You must simply have faith in me.
The Bodhisattva said,
"If one seeks the path to Buddhahood with single-mindedness and without causing harm to others."
He restored [the body] to its former state.
As soon as he had spoken, it was restored.
When humans and devas saw this, they were all filled with great compassion and joy.
"This is truly unprecedented!
He will certainly become a Buddha;
I shall make offerings to him."
Regarding the mark of being filled with corpses:
it was like King Sudāma;
this king was diligent and always relied upon truthful speech.
Just as he was about to enter the park for recreation and had only just exited the city gate,
a certain brāhmaṇa approached and begged him, saying:
"The King is a man of merit who takes pity on my poverty.
The King said,
"You must wait for my return."
Just as he arrived at the garden, there was a king of birds with two wings named Mṛgapāda,
who had made a vow with a mountain deity to seize one thousand kings.
He had already captured nine hundred and ninety-nine kings;
he was lacking only King Śūdraka,
whom [the deity] flew through the air and seized, carrying him away.
The women wailed and lamented, filling the entire garden with their grief.
Śarabha seized the king and brought him to his own dwelling,
placing him among the other kings.
King Sūdamana shed tears like falling rain.
Mṛgāra said, "O great Kṣatriya!"
"Why do you weep like a small child?
For those born there is death; where there is meeting, there must be parting. Sudatta replied, "I am not afraid of death."
"I regret that since birth I have never uttered a falsehood,
yet now I have broken my word.
By promising alms to this brahmin, I have betrayed my long-held resolve and brought upon myself the sin of deception."
Therefore, the deer-footed Tīrṇa said:
"Go back for seven days;
once the offerings are completed, come back to face death."
"If he does not come, I have the power to seize him.
Your Majesty may then freely bestow gifts as you wish and install the crown prince as king."
Having assembled the great multitude of people, the King then apologized, saying:
"My wisdom is not all-encompassing; in minor matters, I have failed to act according to the Dharma."
Seeing this, he became enraged and said, "This body of mine now belongs to no one else; I must depart.
O King, though the people and their kinsmen entreat me to stay, I pray that you will take heed and continue to grant your protection to this kingdom."
"Do not worry about the ghost-king Mṛgāra-pāda.
You should provide protection with an iron house and elite troops;
though Mṛgāra-pāda is divine, he will not fear them."
The King spoke in verse:
"Truthful speech is the foremost precept; truthful speech is the ladder for ascending to heaven;
truthful speech is the greatness of even a small person."
"Lying leads to hell;
I would rather lose my body and life now by guarding truthful speech.
Thereupon, he set out and went to where the Deer-footed One was.
Seeing him coming, they were filled with joy.
"You are a man of truthful speech who does not violate his word of honor;
everyone cherishes their life, yet having escaped, you have now returned."
"You are a great man.
At that time, King Śūdraka extensively praised truthful speech and rebuked false speech.
Upon hearing this, Mṛgacaru’s faith became pure.
He said to Śuddha, "Since you are able to speak thus,
I now release you."
The kings each returned to their own countries.
After these words had been spoken, the kings each departed, and so forth.
As for the characteristics of the accomplishment of patience:
For example, when the Rishi Kṣānti was practicing patience in the forest,
King Kali led his many court ladies there.
Having entered the garden to play and finished eating and drinking, the king took a short nap. While the women were gathering flowers among the trees, they saw this rishi;
they paid him their respects with prostrations and stood to one side.
At that time, the rishi praised loving-kindness and patience to the women;
his words were so exquisite that those who heard them forgot all weariness,
and after a long while, they departed.
Having awakened from his sleep, the king did not see the women; drawing his sword, he followed their tracks and saw them standing before the rishi.
His jealousy flared up intensely, and with eyes blazing with rage, he brandished his sword at the rishi.
"What are you doing? The seer replied, "I am practicing loving-kindness and patience."
The king said,
"I shall now test you;
I will cut off your hands, feet, ears, and nose with a sharp sword."
"If you do not feel anger, then you truly know how to practice patience.
The seer said, "Do as you wish.
The king immediately drew his sword and severed the seer's hands, feet, ears, and nose.
And he asked him,
"Is your mind moved?
He replied:
"I cultivate loving-kindness and patience, so my mind remains unmoved.
The king said, "You are but a single person here; you possess no power."
"Though I speak these words with my mouth, who would believe them?
At that time, the rishi immediately made this vow:
"If it is true that I am one who has cultivated loving-kindness and patience,"
The blood was to become milk;
it immediately transformed into milk.
The king, greatly alarmed, fled with his court ladies.
At that time, the nāga deity of the forest, for the sake of this rishi,
brought down thunder, lightning, and a clap of thunderbolts to inflict a deadly injury upon the king;
consequently, he did not return to the palace, and his marks of perfection reached fullness through his diligent exertion.
It is like Prince Supriya seeking the wish-fulfilling jewel,
as described at the end of the first fascicle;
having obtained the jewel, it fell into the sea, and he then attempted to bale out the great ocean.
Even if my sinews and bones were to wither away,
I would never grow weary or abandon this;
I vow to attain what I desire in order to provide for all sentient beings.
Having relieved his bodily suffering,
the devas questioned him,
and he replied:
They continued their efforts without ceasing.
Seeing this diligence, the devas assisted them in bailing out the ocean;
thus, half of the seawater was diminished.
When the various nāgas saw that the seawater was diminishing, they feared the ocean would run dry;
they sent a pearl to him. As for the marks of one who is full of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*):
For example, there was a conch-crested seer named Śāṇakavāsin.
It is incorrect for someone to depict his image in the form of a monk;
he had attained the fourth dhyāna, wherein inhalation and exhalation cease.
Sitting beneath a tree, he remained perfectly still and motionless.
Seeing him unmoving, a bird mistook him for a log and laid its eggs within the topknot of the seer.
The seer arose from his meditative concentration and perceived an egg upon the crown of his head;
he then reflected within himself.
"If I were to rise from my practice,
the mother bird would never return again and the eggs would surely perish.
He then entered meditative concentration once more until the fledglings flew away.
Thereupon he set out on his journey.
As for the mark of the perfection of *prajñā*,
it is like the minister Gopaka, who divided the land of Jambudvīpa into seven parts.
He causes cities and villages to be all equally distributed in order to quell disputes.
Regarding the marks cultivated over a hundred kalpas:
Having passed through three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, one plants the marks during a hundred kalpas;
"planting" here refers to cultivation.
That is to say, within those hundred kalpas, one cultivates the karma of the marks.
Question:
In what [place] are the seeds and so forth planted? Answer:
It is among the humans of Jambudvīpa within the desire realm, specifically those with male bodies,
when a Buddha has appeared in the world;
for it cannot be planted by others who do not serve as the requisite conditions.
The sixth consciousness is the preparatory karma.
Question:
What is the characteristic of the initial seed?
Answer: Some say it is because,
at the very beginning of planting [the seed], the soles of the feet are level and first established [therein].
Thereafter, one plants the remaining marks.
Some say [the first is] the deep blue eyes.
Because one first regards sentient beings with great compassion,
although there is this statement, its meaning is not necessarily so; when the conditions coincide,
the planting [of seeds] occurs simultaneously, as there is no logical sequence of before and after.
Question:
Is it one volition or many volitions? Answer: [It is] one volition.
A single thought-impulse plants a single mark;
a single mark employs a hundred merits. Question: [What is this?]
"How much constitutes one unit of merit?
Answer: Some say:
The sovereignty over the four continents by a Wheel-Turning King constitutes one merit.
Some say it is like the sovereignty over the two heavens by Śakra, which constitutes one merit.
Some say [it extends] up to the sixth heaven; others say...
The merit possessed by all people, with the exception of those in their final birth before Buddhahood, constitutes a single unit of merit.
Some say that the merit of all sentient beings throughout the great trichiliocosm together constitutes a single unit of merit.
Some say that to cure the blindness of all sentient beings in a great trichiliocosm so that they are healed constitutes a single merit. Others say:
It is said that curing a thousand people by administering poison to them constitutes one merit;
others say that saving a thousand people from death constitutes one merit.
Some say: To be able to preach the Dharma for all people who have broken their precepts and views,
causing them to abandon such things, constitutes one merit.
Some say that there is nothing with which it can be compared;
when a bodhisattva enters the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
Because the mental activities, great practices, seeds, characteristics, causes, and conditions are immeasurable, the merit is likewise immeasurable;
only a Buddha can know this.
The *Śāstra* (Treatise), fascicle 22, further states:
When a bodhisattva cultivates each of the ten wholesome paths of action, there are five levels of mind:
namely, inferior, middling, superior, superior-superior, and superior-middling.
These range from the initial arousal of the five minds up to their full perfection.
Thus, one hundred such mental states are called the "hundred merits" that constitute a single mark.
Continuing in this manner up to thirty-two marks is termed the "purity of the body."
The twenty-second passage of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* is identical [to this].
Those who have attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) do not possess untainted supernormal powers (*anāsravābhijñā*), because they have not yet severed their afflictions (*kleśa*).
The five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) are as explained in the section on the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*). Regarding the thirty-four moments of mind (*citta*),
the interpretation here follows the intent of the treatise (*śāstra*), which differs slightly from the explanations found in various sūtras and śāstras concerning the abandonment [of defilements].
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The various afflictions (*kleśa*) of the lower stages were not severed at the time of their causes;
it was only upon reaching the foot of the tree that [the Bodhisattva] [severed] the nine grades of afflictions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*) belonging to the nine stages."
The general name is nineteen; therefore,
it is said that the stage of the *piṭaka*-bodhisattva is the same as that of ordinary beings,
by means of the nine unimpeded knowledges (*anantarya-jñāna*) and the nine liberations (*vimokṣa*).
These together constitute eighteen.
Within the path of vision (darśanamārga), the eight patiences (kṣānti) and the eight knowledges (jñāna) together comprise sixteen moments of mind.
Taken together, these constitute thirty-four moments of mind.
According to the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Mahāvibhāṣā*,
the afflictions of the lower eight stages have already been abandoned prior to the initial cultivation of dhyāna.
Only in the stage of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) do the nine grades of views and afflictions remain in their entirety.
By means of the nine paths of non-obstruction and the nine paths of liberation,
because its faculties are superior, one no longer further cultivates the meditative concentrations of the eight lower stages.
They differ from the śrāvakas and are distinct from the pratyekabuddhas.
The pratyekabuddha has previously abandoned the afflictions of the eight stages and realized awakening in a single sitting;
he then proceeds to cultivate the ninth stage in successive order.
Furthermore, the two paths— the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*)— arise again.
Although the afflictions are not abandoned within the lower eight stages,
this is because it is the natural order (*dharmatā*) of the sequential progression of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*).
Each stage (bhūmi) possesses eighteen minds;
thus, across the nine stages, there are one hundred and sixty-two minds.
When combined with the sixteen moments of the path of seeing (darśanamārga), this totals one hundred and seventy-eight minds.
The Bodhisattva is not like this;
therefore, there are only thirty-four moments of mind.
This differs from the *Abhidharmakośa*.
The translations by Master Kumārajīva and the intent of Nāgārjuna should both be free from error;
those who disagree with this [should reconsider].
For now, let us resolve this by means of a single interpretation so that the principles of the two treatises may be brought into alignment: according to the *Abhidharmakośa*,
one has already finished abandoning the afflictions (*kleśa*) at the time of practicing dhyāna.
It is not further severed.
According to other schools in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*,
although that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) is severed, it is not yet termed "severed."
Upon reaching the Bodhi tree, one merely cuts off non-perception (*asaṃjñā*).
Both [the eighth stage and the stage at the Bodhi tree] are designated as "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*);
however, they differ only in that their names are derived from their respective categories (*nikāya*).
Therefore, the two treatises differ in their application of meaning.
Furthermore, the scripture states below,
citing the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* that there are six hundred births and cessations in a single thought-moment (*ekacitta-kṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, the masters of the *Abhidharmasamaya* differ in their numerical explanations;
they clarify that even a single moment of thought possesses many moments,
thereby proving the thirty-four moments of mind in the uninterrupted [path].
This does not constitute an obstacle.
In the section following the one immediately preceding this, the distinctions [between the views] were analyzed to establish the Middle Way.
Having illuminated the conventional truth for three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and illuminated the ultimate truth beneath the tree,
he is termed "Doubly Distinct" (*ubhayaviśiṣṭa*) when compared to those before him; he differs from the two vehicles and from bodhisattvas,
as the latter remain at the stage of disciples (*śrāvaka*).
Therefore, it is said that [the teaching] differs from that for disciples, and the three truths are provisionally established.
The Bodhisattva merely illuminates what is below;
this explains the characteristics of the provisionally established Middle Way.
Since it lacks intrinsic nature and exists only as a provisional designation of "middle" based on simultaneous illumination,
and since the designation "middle" is itself provisional, the eye and wisdom that illuminate the middle are likewise provisionally established; therefore,
it is said that they are "further added."
Regarding separation, the following section distinguishes between separation and combination.
This may involve assigning [the relics] to disciples,
or the Buddha himself distributing them.
Since they are already included within the preceding and succeeding [categories], there are only two;
if it were entirely present in the Buddha and absent in others,
it would therefore receive the name of the "Third Truth" in relation to the Buddha.
The reason why the Three Baskets (Tripitaka) are not included within the fivefold Three Truths is that the Middle Way therein lacks a substantial entity.
This follows the passage concerning those of the three vehicles below.
This clarifies the distinctions and unifications of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*).

Although [the two vehicles] are identical in their abandonment [of afflictions], because there are those of sharp faculties among the bodhisattvas, they depart from the Truth (*satya*) to emerge within the Middle Way; therefore, it is said that the Truth is distinct.
Regarding the subsequent citation from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and other texts:
"The wise" refers to those of sharp faculties who, upon seeing the middle way,
are said to see that it is not empty.
"Non-empty" (aśūnya) means not merely empty.
The perfection of the three virtues is called Great Nirvana.
This excludes those of the Two Vehicles and below.
Citing a passage from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*:
"The wisdom of the sun illuminates the center;
those of dull faculties see only emptiness from beginning to end."
The "assembling" (*pihui*) in the *Lotus Sūtra* does not carry the meaning of "opening and closing" (*kaifan*) as used here.
Since the emptiness (*kong*) differs from what follows, this section precisely clarifies the meaning of opening and closing.
However, it is not merely that the name "emptiness" differs from "not-merely-empty.
The knowledge of all things (sarvajñā) illuminates only emptiness;
the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñā) illuminates not-merely-empty.
This is termed the differentiation of wisdom.
Since reality (tattva) inherently contains both [aspects], wisdom likewise possesses these two distinctions.
Within the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), the Middle Way is further differentiated and revealed.
Therefore, it is said that there is a distinction between the two truths;
yet, what is now unified is based on the Shared Teaching (tongjiao), and thus it is said that when the two truths are expounded here, they are merely designated as the "True Truth" (zhendi).
Below the section on the Two Vehicles,
it opens up the sharp and dull faculties of the Bodhisattvas of the Two Vehicles,
distinguishing their contemplations of the Truths (*satya*).
Because they are distinct, there is the sense of being "contained within.

As for the phrase "purifying Buddha-lands," even Bodhisattvas who emerge from the Shared Teaching (tongjiao) into the provisional (chujia) act as causes for purifying lands for the sake of sentient beings.
When one forms karmic connections everywhere, the capacities of sentient beings ripen, habitual tendencies are severed, and Buddhahood is attained;
this is called "purifying the Buddha-field.
At the time of forming these connections, it is called "the practice of purifying the Buddha-field."
Therefore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"Bodhisattvas take up pure lands solely for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings.
Thus it is said: "Generosity is the pure land of a bodhisattva."
When the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood,
all sentient beings capable of renunciation will come to be born in his land;
at the time of forming karmic connections, he gathers them through the practice of giving.
When he attains Buddhahood, the land will abound in rare treasures;
all those capable of renunciation shall be born together in that realm,
where they will receive the five kinds of giving as transformative benefits.
Because there are five distinctions at the time of gathering [beings]— namely, humans, devas, and the four teachings—
all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are none other than the practices for the pure land of a bodhisattva.
Therefore, there are four lands that encompass sentient beings both horizontally and vertically;
this is based on the transitional stages [of practice].
Thus, the meaning of the Pure Land is pervasive across all teachings.
For now, this text follows the perspective of the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), who attain the fruit of the Pure Land by severing their remaining residual habits (*vāsanā*).
This differs from the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*) only in this respect.
As for the meaning of the Pure Land as clarified in the twenty-second fascicle of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*:
It is sufficient to say that if one wishes to encompass their essential meaning, it is universally applicable;
this is likewise true for all teachings regarding the distinct ways of contemplating and gathering in sentient beings.
From the perspective of bodhisattvas of superior faculties...
The phrase "The Bodhisattva of Sharp Faculties clarifies and opens the True [Dharma] from within the Middle" refutes the ancient interpretation;
the *Zhuāngyán* (Ornament) commentary states that it "emerges."
Kaishan said, "It does not emerge.
This is because among those who study the Bodhisattva path shared by the Three Vehicles, there are both those with limited capacity and those with unlimited capacity.
The ancients did not understand these two types of faculties—the sharp and the dull.
They merely dispute whether the fruit of Buddhahood emerges or does not emerge;
they have never yet grasped the underlying intent behind this opening and closing.
Consequently, the two schools each cling to their own respective tenets.
The current texts refute both [positions].
